shots.phrase: Begin by framing Introduction to Processor Architecture as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results.

Consider this worked case: A modern CPU processes instructions by fetching, decoding, and executing them in a pipeline, while classic architectures like the Von Neumann model separate instruction and data storage.
List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion.
Now define Registers and Data Formats precisely enough that another learner could test the definition.
Consider this worked case: In RISC-V, integer registers x1 through x31 hold software-visible values, while x0 always reads as zero, ensuring predictable data handling.
Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them.
With the foundation in place, examine how Instruction Set and Operation Codes operates in a concrete sequence.
Consider this worked case: Load instructions transfer data from memory into registers, while store instructions transfer register data to memory, forming the core data movement mechanism.
Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition.
Next, compare the choices involved in Control Flow and Branching and make the decision criteria explicit.
Consider this worked case: Conditional branches redirect execution to different memory addresses when specific register values meet a condition, enabling loops and decision trees.
Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts.
Apply Memory Hierarchy and Addressing to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition.
Consider this worked case: Direct addressing loads data from a fixed memory address into a register, while indirect addressing uses a register value as the memory address.
indirect addressing with memory maps, showing register-to-memory address resolution steps.
Examine the tradeoffs in User Mode vs.
Analysis distinguishes user mode, privileged kernel code, hardware translation, interrupt state, resource ownership, and synchronization invariants.
On screen, show a two-tier memory model with user space and kernel space, highlighting permission bits and privilege levels.
Stress-test the reasoning around System Calls and Traps with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome.
Consider this worked case: When a process requests file I/O, a system call switches to kernel mode, and a trap captures registers to resume execution after completion.
Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds.
Use Page Tables and Virtual Memory to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action.
Consider this worked case: A page table entry translates a virtual address to a physical frame, with read/write/execute bits controlling access permissions.
Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause.
Connect Scheduling and Context Switching to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system.
Consider this worked case: When a process blocks on I/O, the scheduler picks another runnable process and saves the current processor state for later restoration.
Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations.
Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis.
Consider this worked case: A simulation tracks register values, memory operations, and control flow to verify that architectural state remains consistent across instructions.
For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step.
